passages.happening:
The LORD tells Moses to bring Aaron and his sons, their garments, the anointing oil, a bull, two rams and a basket of unleavened bread, “and assemble the whole congregation at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting” (verse 3). Moses does so, and says to the people, “This is what the LORD has commanded to be done” (verse 5).

“Then Moses presented Aaron and his sons and washed them with water” (verse 6). He dresses Aaron in the tunic, sash, robe and ephod, the breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim, and the turban with its gold plate (verses 7-9).

He anoints the tabernacle and everything in it, and the altar (verses 10-11). “He also poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron’s head and anointed him to consecrate him” (verse 12). Then he dresses Aaron's sons (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
After seven chapters of instruction, Leviticus becomes a story. The offerings need priests, and here they are installed. Every step carries out what God told Moses in Exodus 29. In Exodus the tabernacle was first commanded and then built just as commanded. Now the same happens with the priesthood.

The whole people is gathered to watch. Israel's priests are not made in secret.

The man at the center has a past, and every hearer knew it. Aaron had made the golden calf. Deuteronomy says God was angry enough to destroy him, and that Moses prayed for him. Now Moses washes him, dresses him and anoints him. His office begins in mercy.

Each act marks a change. Washing sets aside the ordinary. The clothes give the office a shape that can be seen. The breastpiece carried twelve stones with the names of the tribes of Israel, so that Aaron bore the people over his heart when he went into the Holy Place. The Urim and Thummim were used to seek God's decision in hard cases. They were probably some kind of sacred lot, though what they looked like is not known.

Anointing with oil marks a person or thing as belonging to God. The Hebrew verb is mashach. From it comes mashiach, ‘anointed one’, the word behind Messiah. Its Greek form is Christos.

Notice what Aaron does in all this. Nothing. He is washed, dressed and anointed by another. In this chapter holiness is given, not earned.

One phrase beats through the chapter like a drum: Moses did ‘as the LORD had commanded him’. It comes six times. What happens here is obedience, not invention.
passages.later:
The instructions were given in Exodus: “In this way you are to ordain Aaron and his sons” (Exodus 29:9).

A psalm remembers the oil: “It is like fine oil on the head, running down on the beard, running down Aaron’s beard over the collar of his robes” (Psalm 133:2).

The letter to the Hebrews draws a lesson from Aaron's call: “No one takes this honor upon himself; he must be called by God, just as Aaron was” (Hebrews 5:4). It says that Christ too was appointed by God.
passages.hard:
Why would God make Aaron, the man who built the golden calf, Israel's high priest?

The difficulty is real. Aaron shaped the calf, built an altar before it, and then told Moses that it simply came out of the fire (Exodus 32:24). This chapter does not mention any of it, and nothing in it suggests that Aaron had earned his office since.

The Bible's own answers point several ways. The priesthood rests on God's choice, made known before the calf (Exodus 28 and 29), and God did not take it back. Aaron was alive only because Moses had pleaded for him (Deuteronomy 9:20). And the ordination begins with a sin offering for Aaron and his sons. The priesthood never pretended that priests were without sin.

Hebrews sees a kindness in that. A human high priest “is able to deal gently with those who are ignorant and misguided, since he himself is beset by weakness” (Hebrews 5:2).
passages.asks: Aaron was washed and clothed by someone else, in front of everyone, with his failure known. Ask whether you believe God can use a person with a past, and whether you believe it of yourself. And ask what you are still trying to earn that can only be given.

passages.t: A sin offering and a burnt offering for the priests
passages.happening:
“Moses then brought the bull near for the sin offering, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head” (verse 14). Moses kills it and puts its blood on the four horns of the altar, “purifying the altar” (verse 15). He burns the fat, and burns the rest of the bull outside the camp (verses 16-17).

Then the ram for the burnt offering. Aaron and his sons lay their hands on its head. Moses kills it, sprinkles the blood on the altar, and burns the whole ram, “a pleasing aroma, an offering made by fire to the LORD” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The first sacrifice of Israel's priesthood is for the priests' own sins. Before Aaron and his sons can make atonement for anyone else, atonement must be made for them. They lay their own hands on the bull.

The blood also cleanses the altar. Verse 15 says Moses purified it and ‘consecrated it so that atonement could be made on it’. The place where Israel will meet God must itself be made ready.

Then comes the burnt offering, the whole gift of chapter 1. The order matters and it will come again in chapter 9: first the offering that deals with sin, then the offering that gives everything to God.

Moses acts as the priest throughout. He had done so before, when the covenant was sealed with blood at Sinai. But his task here is to install the priesthood, not to hold it. After this week the altar belongs to Aaron's family.
passages.later:
The letter to the Hebrews notes this need: a high priest “is obligated to offer sacrifices for his own sins, as well as for the sins of the people” (Hebrews 5:3). It sets Jesus apart at this point, as one who “does not need to offer daily sacrifices, first for His own sins and then for the sins of the people” (Hebrews 7:27).

That contrast is the New Testament's own. It does not slight Aaron's service. As the notes on Hebrews 8 say, a shadow is real.
passages.asks: The priests had to be forgiven before they could serve. Ask whether you try to serve God or others out of a sense that you must make up for something. And ask what it would be like to serve as someone already forgiven.

passages.happening:
“After that, Moses presented the other ram, the ram of ordination, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands on its head” (verse 22).

Moses kills it and puts some of its blood “on Aaron’s right earlobe, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot” (verse 23). He does the same for Aaron's sons (verse 24).

He places the fat, the right thigh and three kinds of bread from the basket in their hands, and they lift them before the LORD as a wave offering. Then he burns them on the altar (verses 25-28). Last, he sprinkles anointing oil and blood from the altar on Aaron and his sons and on their clothes. “So he consecrated Aaron and his garments, as well as Aaron’s sons and their garments” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
This is the offering named at the end of chapter 7 and not explained until now. The Hebrew word for ordination means ‘filling’. To ordain a priest was, in the Hebrew idiom, to fill his hand. Here it happens before our eyes: Moses puts the parts of the offering into the priests' hands.

The blood on the ear, the thumb and the toe is the strangest moment in the chapter. The text does not explain it. Readers have long taken the three as standing for the whole person, from top to bottom, and the right side as the side of honor and strength. Many add that the ear is for hearing God's word, the hand for doing his work and the foot for walking in his ways. That fits the rite well, though the chapter does not say it.

One link is in the book itself. The same three places are marked on a person healed of skin disease when he is brought back into the community (14:14). The priest who is set apart and the outcast who is brought home are marked in the same way.
passages.later:
Leviticus describes the cleansed person: the priest puts blood “on the right earlobe of the one to be cleansed, on the thumb of his right hand, and on the big toe of his right foot” (Leviticus 14:14).

Peter gives the name of priests to all who belong to Christ: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9). Christians differ on how this bears on ordained ministers. Catholic and Orthodox churches call their presbyters priests. Protestant churches, following Luther, generally keep priestly language for Christ and for the whole church. These notes take no side.
passages.asks: Ear, hand and foot were marked for God. Ask what you listen to, what your hands are busy with, and where your feet take you in an ordinary week. And ask which of the three you find hardest to give to God.

passages.t: Seven days at the door of the tent
passages.happening:
Moses tells Aaron and his sons to boil the meat at the entrance to the tent and eat it there with the bread from the basket, and to burn what is left (verses 31-32).

“You must not go outside the entrance to the Tent of Meeting for seven days, until the days of your ordination are complete” (verse 33). “What has been done today has been commanded by the LORD in order to make atonement on your behalf” (verse 34). They are to stay day and night for seven days “and keep the LORD’s charge so that you will not die” (verse 35).

“So Aaron and his sons did everything the LORD had commanded through Moses” (verse 36).
passages.hearers:
The ordination ends with a meal and a week of waiting. The priests eat the ordination offering at the door of the tent. Then they stay there for seven days.

The number seven keeps coming back in this chapter. The altar was sprinkled seven times, and the ordination takes seven days, the length of the first week in Genesis.

The warning ‘so that you will not die’ is sober. To serve close to God is a gift, and it is not safe to treat it lightly. The story is preparing the reader for what happens two chapters on.

The chapter closes with obedience. Aaron and his sons did everything they were told. The story of the priests begins well.
passages.later:
Near the end of the wilderness years the garments passed on. “After Moses had removed Aaron’s garments and put them on his son Eleazar, Aaron died there on top of the mountain” (Numbers 20:28). The office outlived the man.

Hebrews draws out the contrast with a priesthood that passes from one dying man to the next. Of Jesus it says, “He always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7:25).
passages.asks: The priests waited seven days at the door before they began. Ask whether you allow time to be made ready for what God asks of you, or rush to begin. And ask what you are waiting for now, and whether the waiting itself may be part of the work.
